facts.statement: Eschatornis is known from a single species, Eschatornis aterradora, represented by a partial left tibiotarsus.
facts.quote: The genus contains a single species, Eschatornis aterradora, known from a partial left tibiotarsus, a primary lower leg bone of birds.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen MCL-A-1.795 was discovered by Cástor Cartelle in the Toca dos Ossos cave in Bahia, Brazil.
facts.quote: The Eschatornis holotype specimen, MCL-A-1.795, was discovered and collected by Cástor Cartelle in the Toca dos Ossos cave of the Caatinga Formation in Bahia, Brazil.

facts.statement: In 2008, Herculano Alvarenga and colleagues tentatively classified the fossil as an indeterminate species of Cathartidae.
facts.quote: It was first tentatively classified as an indeterminate species of the family Cathartidae (New world vultures) by the Brazilian ornithologist Herculano Alvarenga and colleagues in 2008 pending further examination.

facts.statement: Victor Hugo M. Machado and colleagues described Eschatornis aterradora as a new genus and species in 2026.
facts.quote: In 2026, the Brazilian paleontologist Victor Hugo M. Machado and colleagues redescribed this fossil as a new genus and species of psilopterine phorusrhacid, Eschatornis aterradora.

facts.statement: The name Eschatornis combines Greek and Latin words meaning "last bird" because it was thought to be the latest known phorusrhacid.
facts.quote: The generic name, Eschatornis, is derived from the Greek word ἔσχατος (éschatos, "last") and the Latin word ornis meaning "bird", since this taxon possibly represents the latest known phorusrhacid at the time of description.

facts.statement: The specific name aterradora means "terrifying" in Portuguese and Spanish, referencing the common name for terror birds.
facts.quote: The Latinized specific name, aterradora, is derived from the word meaning "terrifying" in Portuguese and Spanish, in reference to the popular name of phorusrhacids, the terror birds.

facts.statement: The tibiotarsus morphology is consistent with the family Phorusrhacidae and resembles the subfamilies Psilopterinae and Mesembriornithinae.
facts.quote: The morphology (shape) of the tibiotarsus is consistent with that of the family Phorusrhacidae, especially resembling that of the relatively small-sized subfamilies Psilopterinae and Mesembriornithinae.

facts.statement: Eschatornis is an extinct genus of phorusrhacid, also known as a terror bird.
facts.quote: Eschatornis () is an extinct genus of phorusrhacid (terror bird) from the Late Pleistocene of northeastern Brazil.

facts.statement: Features like an oblique supratendinal bridge and an oval opening on the extensor sulcus link the fossil to phorusrhacids rather than cathartids.
facts.quote: Re-examination in 2026 noted that some of the features in the distal end of the tibiotarsus, originally used for its tentative identification as a cathartid in 2008, are also found in phorusrhacids such as the supratendinal bridge (critical bony bridge) being oblique, albeit to a lesser extent than that of Psilopterus, and the oval opening on the extensor sulcus (shallow groove).

facts.statement: Eschatornis lived approximately 25,326 to 25,733 calibrated years Before Present, potentially extending the known range of phorusrhacids into the Late Pleistocene.
facts.quote: It is the first purported Late Pleistocene phorusrhacid fossil to be directly dated using radiocarbon dating, approximately 25,326-25,733 calibrated (cal.) years Before Present, possibly extending the known occurrence of phorusrhacids during the Pleistocene epoch.

facts.statement: Carbon isotope analysis suggests Eschatornis lived in a mesic, arboreal savannah habitat rich in plants.
facts.quote: Carbon isotope signature obtained from the holotype suggested that Eschatornis lived in a mesic, arboreal savannah (mixed woodland-grassland) habitat rich in plants.

rejected.quote: The holotype of Eschatornis is estimated to have weighed approximately or less than 6.1 kg based on minimal tibiotarsus circumference, similar in size to the related Psilopterus.
